(CNN) — Polygamist sect leader Warren Jeffs attempted to hang himself earlier this year while jailed awaiting trial, according to court documents unsealed Tuesday by a Utah judge.

Jeffs, the leader and self-proclaimed prophet of the 10,000-member Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, is awaiting sentencing after being convicted on two counts of being an accomplice to rape.

The documents, released by Fifth District Judge James Shumate at the request of the media, also indicate that Jeffs confessed to “immorality” with a “sister” and a daughter more than 30 years ago.

Among the records is an April competency report on Jeffs, in which social worker Eric Nielsen wrote that throughout January, Jeffs refused food and drink and developed ulcers on his knees from kneeling in prayer for hours. On January 28, the report said, he attempted to hang himself in his cell.

In the days following the suicide attempt, while under suicide watch, Jeffs on separate occasions threw himself against a wall and banged his head against it.

Jail transcripts show that Jeffs’ suicide attempt came three days after a visit with his brother, Nephi, during which he said, “I am not the prophet. I never was the prophet, and I have been deceived by the powers of evil ... I ask for everyone’s forgiveness.”

Jeffs also told his brother, “Farewell forever.”

The day before that, Jeffs told a follower in a phone conversation that he was “covered with immorality with a sister and a daughter when I was younger.” In the FLDS, members refer to adult women as “sister,” and Jeffs’ meaning was unclear.

Jeffs’ defense attorneys, who opposed the release of the documents, said in a motion objecting to the unsealing of the statements that Jeffs recanted them the following month.

Defense attorneys contend that Jeffs’ medical condition affected his state of mind when the statements were made. They presented Shumate with a letter from another Jeffs attorney arguing that the release of the statements could influence an Arizona jury when Jeffs stands trial in that state.

Jeffs, 51, was convicted in September of being an accomplice to rape. He was accused of using his religious influence over his followers to coerce a 14-year-old girl into marriage with her 19-year-old cousin. He faces a sentence of up to life in prison when he is sentenced November 20.

The FLDS, which is not affiliated with the mainstream Mormon church, is based in the neighboring border towns of Hildale, Utah, and Colorado City, Arizona.

Jeffs, a former school headmaster, is the son of the sect’s previous president and “prophet,” Rulon Jeffs, who died in 2002. Jeffs was on the FBI’s 10 Most Wanted Fugitives list when he was arrested in August 2006 outside Las Vegas, Nevada.

Critics say that within the FLDS, marriages are arranged for girls as young as 13, and competition for brides may be reduced by exiling male teenagers and young men. If male followers are excommunicated, critics allege, their wives and children can be reassigned.

During Jeffs’ trial, defense attorneys argued that authorities were persecuting him because of his religious beliefs, including the practice of polygamy as a path to heaven.

If Jeffs disavowed his role as prophet of the FLDS, it could create upheaval within the secretive sect. However, two of his followers who spoke to CNN—despite FLDS members typically avoiding contact with reporters—said they do not believe he made the statements.

“He is a perfectly priestly man,” said a woman who identified herself as Cathy. “He is a man of God, and we will always love him. Once a prophet, always a prophet.”

Her husband, Patrick, told CNN, “It’s hogwash. I don’t believe it ... I will always consider him my prophet.”

CNN’s Gary Tuchman contributed to this report.

**BREAKING NEWS: Warren Jeffs Attempts Suicide in Jail as Transcripts Reveal Private Confessions, Shaking FLDS Followers**

**By Staff Writer**  
**St. George, Utah / Kingman, Arizona —** Warren Steed Jeffs, the imprisoned leader of the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints, attempted suicide while in custody, authorities said, adding a dramatic new turn to the legal and spiritual crisis surrounding one of the nation’s most controversial religious figures.

Jeffs, who has led the polygamous FLDS church since the death of his father, Rulon Jeffs, was found in distress in his jail cell and received emergency medical attention, officials said. Authorities declined to provide extensive details, citing privacy and jail-security concerns, but said Jeffs survived and was placed under heightened observation.

The incident comes as court transcripts and recordings have surfaced revealing Jeffs’ startling private statements to followers and family members — statements that appear to include admissions of wrongdoing, spiritual failure and conduct that even some within his own insular community have struggled to reconcile with his prophetic status.

The revelations have intensified turmoil inside the FLDS, a breakaway Mormon sect long based along the Utah-Arizona border in the twin communities of Hildale, Utah, and Colorado City, Arizona, and later centered in part at the church’s Yearning for Zion ranch in Texas.

## Transcripts Describe Confessions and Spiritual Crisis

According to transcripts reviewed in connection with court proceedings, Jeffs made a series of emotional statements in which he suggested he was not the righteous prophet his followers believed him to be. In the transcripts, Jeffs appears to confess to moral and sexual misconduct and repeatedly portrays himself as fallen, unworthy and under divine judgment.

The statements stunned both prosecutors and observers because Jeffs had long maintained near-total religious authority over the FLDS community, where followers regarded him as “the Prophet” and God’s mouthpiece on Earth.

In some passages, Jeffs reportedly told close associates that he had committed “immoral” acts and that God had rejected him. Other portions suggest he believed he had failed to properly lead the church. The transcripts also indicate that Jeffs urged others to make certain disclosures and reconsider his role — though the meaning and sincerity of those statements remain disputed among former members, legal analysts and current followers.

Prosecutors have argued that Jeffs used religious authority to control marriages, families and sexual access within the FLDS community. Defense attorneys and loyal followers have historically characterized the state’s actions against him as religious persecution.

## A Leader Already Facing Serious Charges

Jeffs’ suicide attempt occurred while he was in custody on charges tied to his role in arranging marriages involving underage girls. At the time of his arrest, he was one of the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted fugitives after evading authorities for months.

He was later convicted in Utah as an accomplice to rape for his role in arranging a marriage between a teenage girl and an older man, though that conviction was subsequently overturned on appeal. He was later convicted in Texas of sexually assaulting underage girls he had taken as “spiritual wives” and was sentenced to life in prison.

The latest jail incident underscores the instability surrounding Jeffs’ legal fight and the broader upheaval within the FLDS world, where his authority has remained powerful even from behind bars.

## FLDS Background: Isolation, Polygamy and Prophetic Control

The FLDS traces its origins to early Mormon fundamentalists who rejected the mainstream Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints’ 1890 decision to abandon plural marriage. The mainstream LDS Church has repeatedly emphasized that it has no affiliation with the FLDS and excommunicates members who practice polygamy.

For generations, FLDS members lived in isolated communities, practiced plural marriage and followed a strict hierarchy centered on priesthood authority. Under Rulon Jeffs and later Warren Jeffs, the church became increasingly centralized and authoritarian, according to former members.

Warren Jeffs controlled marriages, reassigned wives and children, excommunicated men, and dictated rules on dress, schooling, work and family life, former followers have said. Critics allege he separated families and expelled young men deemed disobedient or spiritually unworthy, creating a group of so-called “lost boys” pushed out of the community.

Supporters, however, have described Jeffs as a persecuted religious leader targeted for practicing a faith unpopular with outsiders.

## Followers React With Shock, Denial and Prayer

Reaction among FLDS followers was mixed and difficult to gauge because the community remains highly closed to outsiders. Some current members reportedly dismissed the transcripts as manipulated, misunderstood or spiritually misinterpreted. Others said Jeffs’ suffering was part of a divine test.

“He is still the Prophet,” said one supporter familiar with FLDS teachings, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of church discipline. “The world does not understand him. This is persecution.”

Former members responded differently, saying the transcripts confirm what they have long alleged: that Jeffs’ public image as a holy man concealed abuse and manipulation.

“This is what happens when one man is given absolute power over every part of people’s lives,” said one former FLDS member. “People were taught to obey him as if his words came directly from God.”

Some relatives of FLDS members said the suicide attempt may deepen the confusion inside the church. For loyal believers, Jeffs’ apparent despair could be explained as spiritual warfare or martyrdom. For wavering members, however, the confessions could become a breaking point.

“Many people inside have sacrificed everything for him — marriages, children, homes, their entire identity,” said a former member who now assists people leaving the sect. “If they accept that he lied or abused his power, their whole world collapses.”

## Authorities Tighten Watch

Jail officials said Jeffs is being monitored and evaluated. Legal proceedings are expected to continue, though the suicide attempt may prompt questions about his mental health, competency and ability to participate in his defense.

Experts on high-control religious groups said the moment is significant not only legally but psychologically for FLDS members.

“When a prophetic leader shows vulnerability or confesses wrongdoing, followers often split into camps,” said one scholar of new religious movements. “Some double down. Some reinterpret the confession as a test. Others begin to leave.”

For now, Jeffs remains alive, in custody and under scrutiny — a once-commanding religious figure whose private words, public prosecution and attempted self-harm have thrown his already fractured church into deeper uncertainty.

**Jeffs convicted in Utah rape-accomplice trial; competency report cited in court**

*ST. GEORGE, Utah — September 2007* — Warren Jeffs, the reclusive leader of a polygamist sect whose followers regard him as a prophet, was convicted Tuesday on two counts of being an accomplice to rape for his role in arranging the marriage of a 14-year-old girl to her 19-year-old cousin.

Jurors in Washington County, Utah, reached the verdict after a trial that offered a rare look inside the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, or FLDS, a breakaway Mormon sect that practices polygamy and lives largely apart from mainstream society.

Jeffs, 51, showed little emotion as the verdict was read. He faces the possibility of a lengthy prison sentence.

Prosecutors said Jeffs used his religious authority to pressure the teenage girl into a marriage she did not want and then instructed her to “submit” to her husband. The girl, now an adult, testified that she repeatedly objected to the union and told Jeffs she did not want to have sexual relations with her husband.

“The defendant was not merely present,” prosecutors argued during the trial. “He was the one who made this happen.”

Defense attorneys said Jeffs did not commit rape and argued that the case improperly criminalized religious counseling and a spiritual marriage ceremony. They said the young woman’s husband — not Jeffs — was responsible for what happened afterward.

## Competency report raised before trial

Before the case moved forward, questions about Jeffs’ physical and mental condition surfaced in court. A competency report reviewed by the court concluded that Jeffs was able to understand the proceedings and assist in his defense, allowing the trial to continue.

Jeffs had spent months in custody after being captured in Nevada in 2006 following a place on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted list. Authorities had sought him in connection with allegations involving underage marriages within the FLDS community.

Court officials said the competency issue did not prevent the prosecution from proceeding, and the judge allowed jurors to hear testimony from the woman at the center of the case, former FLDS member Elissa Wall.

## FLDS community under scrutiny

The FLDS church is based in the twin border communities of Hildale, Utah, and Colorado City, Arizona. The sect split from the mainstream Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, which abandoned polygamy more than a century ago and has repeatedly said it has no connection to the FLDS.

Jeffs became president of the FLDS after the death of his father, Rulon Jeffs. Former members have described him as wielding near-total control over followers’ marriages, homes, property and spiritual standing.

Critics say the church’s system allowed older men to take multiple wives, including underage girls, while young men were sometimes pushed out of the community. FLDS members and supporters have said outsiders misunderstand their faith and persecute them for their religious beliefs.

Outside the courthouse, a small group of Jeffs supporters stood quietly after the verdict. Some declined to give their full names, citing fear of harassment.

“He is a prophet of God, and we will stand by him,” one supporter said.

Another said the trial was “about our religion, not justice.”

“We believe Brother Jeffs has been wrongly judged by the world,” the supporter said. “The Lord will judge in the end.”

Former FLDS members, however, said the verdict marked a turning point.

“For years, people said nothing could be done,” one former member said. “Today showed that the law can reach inside those walls.”

## Sentencing ahead

Jeffs’ attorneys said they would consider an appeal. Prosecutors said the verdict validated the testimony of the young woman and other former members who came forward despite pressure from the community.
